screens.title: Raspberry Pi as an IoT Gateway and Data Logger
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how a Raspberry Pi can act as the resilient gateway at the edge of an IoT system. A gateway collects readings from sensors, stores them locally when networks are unreliable, and forwards data to the cloud when connectivity allows. We will focus on a practical, file‑based approach using SQLite for durable local storage, a simple retry pattern to avoid data loss, and a lightweight Flask server to present recent readings on a local dashboard. You will see concrete code examples for creating the sensor table, inserting readings, marking records as sent, and scanning unsent rows to retry uploads. You will also explore how WAL mode improves reliability on sudden power loss and why a sent flag is essential for eventual consistency. Finally, the lesson ties these pieces together in the hands‑on activity: build the logger, simulate a network outage, and verify that buffered data uploads after reconnection. By the end you’ll understand the practical tradeoffs of local buffering, how to implement safe inserts and retries, and why separation of collection, storage, and presentation makes systems easier to test and recover. Consider: how would you detect and alert on stuck unsent rows in your system?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Raspberry Pi Gateway
Raspberry Pi as an IoT Gateway and Data Logger
Collect sensor data, buffer it locally with SQLite, retry uploads, and serve a local Flask dashboard.
Orientation

You will learn how to create a small, reliable system: sensors → Raspberry Pi → local SQLite buffer → cloud. The Pi also runs a Flask web server that serves recent readings and a JSON API for charts. The architecture prioritizes durability, simple recovery, and local visibility.

In this lesson

Design the database schema, implement buffering and retry logic, and expose data through Flask for a local dashboard.

Why this matters

Network outages are inevitable. Local storage plus retries ensure no sensor readings are lost and that your system can recover without manual intervention.

Explore Key Topics
SQLite Storage
File-based, serverless database for durable local logging and SQL queries for analytics.
Buffering & Retry
Store readings locally, mark them sent on success, and rescan unsent rows to retry uploads.
Local Dashboard
A Flask server exposes a table and a JSON endpoint for real-time charts on the local network.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter sets four concrete objectives that you will be able to verify by the end of the lab. First, you will design a Raspberry Pi based data logger that collects, stores, and forwards sensor data. That means choosing a schema, writing code to read sensors, and confirming data moves from the Pi to a remote service or local dashboard. Second, you will use SQLite for local storage. You will create tables, insert readings, query recent rows, and enable WAL mode so that writes remain safe across interruptions. Third, you will implement buffering and retry logic. The goal is to ensure that when the network is unreliable, readings are persisted locally, flagged as unsent, and retried later until successful. Fourth, you will run a Flask web server on the Pi that serves a dashboard and a JSON A P I endpoint so you can visualize recent readings from any device on your network. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone so you can test that the system actually stores, buffers, retries, and serves data as intended.

screens.narratorSegment: This companion objectives slide explains how to verify each skill in practice. For the data logger design objective, a practical milestone is a working loop that writes a timestamp, sensor ID, and value into a SQLite table every ten seconds. screens.title: The Gateway Role of the Raspberry Pi
screens.narratorSegment: A gateway is the intermediary that connects low‑power or local sensors to remote cloud services. On a Raspberry Pi, that role combines several responsibilities: collect readings from multiple sensors, normalize them into a common schema, persist them reliably on local storage, and forward them to the cloud. This chapter emphasizes three gateway responsibilities you must design for: durability, observability, and graceful degradation. Durability means writes are safe on the Pi even if power is removed briefly; we rely on SQLite and WAL mode for this. Observability means you can inspect recent readings via S Q L queries or a web UI to diagnose issues. Graceful degradation means the system continues collecting and storing data while the network is down, and then uploads later via a retry process. A common misconception is treating the Pi as a thin forwarder; instead, design the Pi to be the authoritative short‑term store so the system does not lose data. For example, a Pi receiving temperature readings should write each timestamped reading to disk immediately and only mark it sent when confirmation from the cloud arrives. Takeaway: treat the Pi as the reliable buffer that enforces eventual consistency across intermittent networks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Gateway Role
Definition

A gateway collects sensor data, performs local processing and storage, and forwards data to cloud services while handling network failures gracefully.

Durability
Persist readings immediately to prevent loss on power failure.
Observability
Expose recent data via SQL or a local web UI for debugging and verification.
Graceful degradation
Continue to collect and buffer when connectivity is lost, then retry uploads later.
Key Takeaway

Design the Pi as the authoritative short‑term store: write first, send later.

Architecture Snapshot
Sensors
Multiple sensor inputs, serial, I2C, or ADC, normalized to a common format.
Raspberry Pi
  • Store readings in SQLite
  • Run retry loop for unsent rows
  • Host Flask dashboard
Cloud
Receive forwarded events; Pi ensures eventual delivery.
Concrete example
A temperature sensor sends readings every 10 seconds; the Pi writes each reading to a table with timestamp and sensor id, then attempts to POST it to the cloud. If the POST fails, the row remains unsent and the retry loop will resend it later.

screens.title: SQLite for Local IoT Data Storage
screens.narratorSegment: SQLite is a small, file‑based relational database ideal for IoT logging because it requires no separate server process and stores all data in a single file. In practice, this simplicity makes deployment and backups straightforward: copying the. db file moves the data. For sensor logging we typically create a table with columns such as timestamp, sensor_id, value, and a sent flag to indicate cloud delivery status. One practical detail is WAL, or Write‑Ahead Logging, which increases resilience against corruption by recording writes before they are applied to the main file. A common misconception is that file‑based databases are fragile; in fact, when configured with WAL and used with proper commits they provide ACID guarantees suitable for many embedded scenarios. For example, create a simple table and insert a reading using the supplied Python code. Querying the last few rows with ORDER BY timestamp DESC lets you verify the logger is working. Takeaway: SQLite gives you queryable, durable storage without the operational cost of running a database server on the Pi. SQLite for Local IoT Data Storage means serverless, portable, and durable when using wal, making it well suited for local iot data logging and recovery.. In practical terms, why sqlite is a practical choice for embedded logging. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › SQLite Storage
Core benefits
  • Serverless: no separate process to install, ideal for small systems.
  • Durable: WAL mode guards against corruption on power loss.
  • Queryable: SQL lets you filter, aggregate, and inspect readings.
  • Portable: the .db file is easy to copy or back up.
Schema suggestion
Create a sensor_readings table with timestamp TEXT, sensor_id TEXT, value REAL, sent INTEGER DEFAULT 0.
Common misconception

Assuming a plain text file is equivalent. Text files need manual parsing, are hard to query, and are more vulnerable to corruption during interrupted writes.

Concrete example
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime

conn = sqlite3.connect('iot_data.db')
c = conn.cursor()
c.execute('''CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sensor_readings
             (timestamp TEXT, sensor_id TEXT, value REAL, sent INTEGER DEFAULT 0)''')
conn.commit()

# Insert a reading
timestamp = datetime.now().isoformat()
c.execute("INSERT INTO sensor_readings VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
          (timestamp, "TEMP_01", 25.5, 0))
conn.commit()
conn.close()
Run PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL to enable WAL. Verify with PRAGMA journal_mode; it should return WAL.

screens.title: Buffering and Retry Logic
screens.narratorSegment: Buffering and retry logic is the heart of reliability when networks are unreliable. The standard pattern has five steps: 1) store every sensor reading in local SQLite; 2) attempt to send the reading to the cloud; 3) if the send succeeds, mark that row as sent; 4) if the send fails, leave the row unsent; and 5) periodically scan the database for unsent rows and try again. Implement this as a short loop that runs at a controlled cadence — for example, reading sensors every ten seconds and running the retry loop every minute. A common pitfall is continuously hammering a failing network endpoint; to avoid this, stop a retry batch on the first failure or implement exponential backoff. A concrete example is a function that queries rows with sent = 0 and attempts to POST them; on a successful HTTP 200, update sent to 1. Misconception: retries alone don't guarantee order; if ordering matters, include sequence numbers or rely on timestamps and idempotent server handling. Takeaway: the local database becomes a durable queue and the retry loop ensures eventual delivery when connectivity returns.

keyIdea.title: Retry pattern
keyIdea.text: Store first, attempt send, mark on success, and rescan unsent rows later; avoid aggressive retries on failure.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Buffer & Retry
Five-step pattern
  1. Write every reading to SQLite with sent = 0.
  2. Attempt to send readings to the cloud endpoint.
  3. On success, update the row to sent = 1.
  4. On failure, leave the row and defer retry.
  5. Periodically scan and retry unsent rows until they succeed.
Backoff & batching
Stop a retry batch on first failure to avoid overwhelming a downed connection, and implement increasing delays between attempts if failures persist.
Concrete scenario
If your Pi loses internet for an hour, readings accumulate locally with sent=0. When the connection returns, the retry loop reads unsent rows and uploads them one by one, marking each as sent to prevent duplication.
Common mistake

Repeatedly retrying without delay or a stop condition can flood the network and hide the real failure cause. Design retries to be respectful of the network state.

screens.title: process_unsent: Resending Unsent Rows
screens.narratorSegment: The process_unsent function demonstrates scanning unsent rows and attempting to send them to the cloud. The function selects rowid, timestamp, sensor_id, and value from sensor_readings where sent = 0. For each row, it calls a send_to_cloud helper that performs an HTTP POST and returns a boolean success flag. On success, the code updates the row to sent = 1 and commits the change; on failure it logs and stops the current batch to avoid flooding the network. Important practical notes: use rowid or a primary key when updating to avoid ambiguous updates, keep the commit after each successful update to make progress durable, and include a short timeout on network calls so the retry loop doesn't hang. A common misconception is that you must resend everything in a single transaction — don’t. Resend operations should be per-row or per-batch so that partial progress is saved. keyIdea.text: Select unsent rows, attempt send, update sent on success, and commit frequently to make progress durable and observable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › process_unsent
Retry loop example
def process_unsent():
    conn = sqlite3.connect('iot_data.db')
    c = conn.cursor()
    c.execute("SELECT rowid, timestamp, sensor_id, value FROM sensor_readings WHERE sent = 0")
    rows = c.fetchall()

    for row in rows:
        rowid, timestamp, sensor_id, value = row
        if send_to_cloud(timestamp, sensor_id, value):
            c.execute("UPDATE sensor_readings SET sent = 1 WHERE rowid = ?", (rowid,))
            conn.commit()
        else:
            break

    conn.close()
Note: break on failure prevents hammering. Consider resuming later with backoff or limiting per-pass attempts.
Practical notes
  • Use rowid or a primary key to update specific rows.
  • Commit after each successful update to record progress.
  • Set HTTP timeouts so the loop does not block indefinitely.
Key Takeaway

Keep retries idempotent and commit frequently so the system can recover and continue from where it left off.

screens.title: Failure Modes and Retry Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding failure modes helps you choose retry behavior. Three common failure types are transient network blips, persistent endpoint errors, and local resource constraints. For transient blips, a simple periodic retry loop with short pauses is effective. For persistent errors like a server returning 5xx responses, the system should apply exponential backoff and alert operators if retries exceed thresholds. For local resource issues, such as low disk space, the Pi should stop collecting temporarily or rotate logs to avoid losing older data. A frequent misconception is to treat all failures the same — this leads to inefficient retries or lost observability. A small comparison: aggressive immediate retries on a downed endpoint waste power and bandwidth; controlled batching with backoff preserves resources and ships data when the server returns. Example: stop retrying on repeated failure and escalate to a log or LED indicator on the Pi, then resume normal retries after a longer wait. Takeaway: design retry strategies to match likely failure causes and preserve system health while ensuring eventual delivery. Failure Modes and Retry Strategies means use short retries for transients, exponential backoff for persistent server errors, and resource checks when local constraints appear.. In practical terms, when to stop, back off, and resume sending data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A frequent misconception is to treat all failures the same — this leads to inefficient retries or lost observability. A small comparison: aggressive immediate retries on a downed endpoint waste power and bandwidth; controlled batching with backoff preserves resources and ships data when the server returns. Example: stop retrying on repeated failure and escalate to a log or LED indicator on the Pi, then resume normal retries after a longer wait. Takeaway: design retry strategies to match likely failure causes and preserve system health while ensuring eventual delivery. Failure types

  • Persistent: server errors — use exponential backoff and alert.

Practical rule
Stop aggressive retries quickly. Prefer a capped retry batch and increase delay between full passes if failures persist.

If the cloud returns errors for several attempts, mark the condition and back off: wait several minutes before the next batch, and generate an alert so maintenance can investigate.

Treating every network failure as identical leads to wasted retries and hidden systemic problems. Different failures need different responses.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.3 › Flask Dashboard
Flask essentials
Define routes for the dashboard and for an API endpoint. Query SQLite for recent rows and pass them to the template or jsonify them for client consumption. Bind to 0.0.0.0 to allow other devices on your LAN to connect.
from flask import Flask, render_template, jsonify
import sqlite3

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/')
def dashboard():
    conn = sqlite3.connect('iot_data.db')
    c = conn.cursor()
    c.execute("SELECT * FROM sensor_readings ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 20")
    data = c.fetchall()
    conn.close()
    return render_template('dashboard.html', readings=data)

@app.route('/api/data')
def api_data():
    conn = sqlite3.connect('iot_data.db')
    c = conn.cursor()
    c.execute("SELECT timestamp, value FROM sensor_readings WHERE sensor_id = 'TEMP_01' ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 100")
    data = c.fetchall()
    conn.close()
    return jsonify(data)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000, debug=False)
Client visualization
The /api/data route returns JSON that a browser can fetch and render with a charting library to display recent trends. Serving raw JSON keeps the server simple and lets the client handle rendering.
Key Tip

Use a small client-side chart and poll the JSON endpoint on an interval to update the view without reloading the page.

screens.title: Separation of Concerns: Collection, Storage, Presentation
screens.narratorSegment: Separation of concerns states that collection, storage, and presentation should be distinct parts of your system. On the Raspberry Pi, keep the sensor read loop focused on capturing and persisting data, the storage layer focused on reliable writes and querying, and the presentation layer focused on rendering data for users or APIs. This separation reduces bugs: for example, if the dashboard slows down, it should not block sensor writes. A common error is coupling read loops with network uploads directly, which can cause missed readings when the network blocks. Instead, write to SQLite immediately and let a separate retry process handle uploads. This design also simplifies testing: you can test the read loop by verifying database inserts, test the retry loop by simulating failures and checking sent flags, and test the dashboard by mocking database queries. Practical example: run the sensor loop as a scheduled process or systemd service, run the retry loop on a cadence, and run Flask as a separate process. Takeaway: clear boundaries lead to safer failure modes and simpler debugging. In practical terms, design rule that keeps your gateway maintainable and testable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how a Raspberry Pi can act as the resilient gateway at the edge of an IoT system. A gateway collects readings from sensors, stores them locally when networks are unreliable, and forwards data to the cloud when connectivity allows. We will focus on a practical, file‑based approach using SQLite for durable local storage, a simple retry pattern to avoid data loss, and a lightweight Flask server to present recent readings on a local dashboard. You will see concrete code examples for creating the sensor table, inserting readings, marking records as sent, and scanning unsent rows to retry uploads. You will also explore how WAL mode improves reliability on sudden power loss and why a sent flag is essential for eventual consistency. Finally, the lesson ties these pieces together in the hands‑on activity: build the logger, simulate a network outage, and verify that buffered data uploads after reconnection. By the end you’ll understand the practical tradeoffs of local buffering, how to implement safe inserts and retries, and why separation of collection, storage, and presentation makes systems easier to test and recover. Consider: how would you detect and alert on stuck unsent rows in your system?

This chapter sets four concrete objectives that you will be able to verify by the end of the lab. First, you will design a Raspberry Pi based data logger that collects, stores, and forwards sensor data. That means choosing a schema, writing code to read sensors, and confirming data moves from the Pi to a remote service or local dashboard. Second, you will use SQLite for local storage. You will create tables, insert readings, query recent rows, and enable WAL mode so that writes remain safe across interruptions. Third, you will implement buffering and retry logic. The goal is to ensure that when the network is unreliable, readings are persisted locally, flagged as unsent, and retried later until successful. Fourth, you will run a Flask web server on the Pi that serves a dashboard and a JSON A P I endpoint so you can visualize recent readings from any device on your network. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone so you can test that the system actually stores, buffers, retries, and serves data as intended.

This companion objectives slide explains how to verify each skill in practice. For the data logger design objective, a practical milestone is a working loop that writes a timestamp, sensor ID, and value into a SQLite table every ten seconds. For SQLite usage, a milestone is to open the database, run a SELECT to retrieve the last 20 rows, and confirm WAL mode is enabled so that sudden power loss does not corrupt the file. For buffering and retry logic, a milestone is to mark records with a sent flag, simulate a failed upload, and see unsent rows persist and later become sent when the network returns. For the Flask dashboard, a milestone is to load the Pi’s IP and view a table of recent readings and a JSON endpoint at /api/data returning the expected time-value pairs. Each of these milestones emphasizes a testable outcome rather than just code: you must observe stored rows, observe retry attempts, and access the local UI. This approach makes it clear whether the system meets the core reliability goals and where you might add alerts or cleanup.

A gateway is the intermediary that connects low‑power or local sensors to remote cloud services. On a Raspberry Pi, that role combines several responsibilities: collect readings from multiple sensors, normalize them into a common schema, persist them reliably on local storage, and forward them to the cloud. This chapter emphasizes three gateway responsibilities you must design for: durability, observability, and graceful degradation. Durability means writes are safe on the Pi even if power is removed briefly; we rely on SQLite and WAL mode for this. Observability means you can inspect recent readings via S Q L queries or a web UI to diagnose issues. Graceful degradation means the system continues collecting and storing data while the network is down, and then uploads later via a retry process. A common misconception is treating the Pi as a thin forwarder; instead, design the Pi to be the authoritative short‑term store so the system does not lose data. For example, a Pi receiving temperature readings should write each timestamped reading to disk immediately and only mark it sent when confirmation from the cloud arrives. Takeaway: treat the Pi as the reliable buffer that enforces eventual consistency across intermittent networks.

SQLite is a small, file‑based relational database ideal for IoT logging because it requires no separate server process and stores all data in a single file. In practice, this simplicity makes deployment and backups straightforward: copying the. db file moves the data. For sensor logging we typically create a table with columns such as timestamp, sensor_id, value, and a sent flag to indicate cloud delivery status. One practical detail is WAL, or Write‑Ahead Logging, which increases resilience against corruption by recording writes before they are applied to the main file. A common misconception is that file‑based databases are fragile; in fact, when configured with WAL and used with proper commits they provide ACID guarantees suitable for many embedded scenarios. For example, create a simple table and insert a reading using the supplied Python code. Querying the last few rows with ORDER BY timestamp DESC lets you verify the logger is working. Takeaway: SQLite gives you queryable, durable storage without the operational cost of running a database server on the Pi. SQLite for Local IoT Data Storage means serverless, portable, and durable when using wal, making it well suited for local iot data logging and recovery.. In practical terms, why sqlite is a practical choice for embedded logging. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the basic Python code to create a sensor_readings table, insert a reading, and query the most recent rows. The supplied code opens a connection to a local file named iot_data. db, creates the table if it doesn't exist, commits, inserts a timestamped reading with a sensor identifier and a numeric value, and closes the connection. A best practice is to keep transactions short: open, write, commit, and close so locks are brief. When querying, use ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT N to inspect the newest readings. A common mistake is not including a sent flag; without it you cannot distinguish uploaded rows from buffered ones. In a concrete example, you insert a temperature reading and later run a SELECT to see the last ten entries. Remember to enable WAL mode for increased resilience. Takeaway: small, clear transactions and an explicit sent flag make safe, testable logging on the Pi. Creating and Querying the SQLite Logger means keep commits short, include a sent flag, and use order by timestamp to inspect recent readings.. In practical terms, a step‑by‑step look at creating the table, inserting readings, and querying recent data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Buffering and retry logic is the heart of reliability when networks are unreliable. The standard pattern has five steps: 1) store every sensor reading in local SQLite; 2) attempt to send the reading to the cloud; 3) if the send succeeds, mark that row as sent; 4) if the send fails, leave the row unsent; and 5) periodically scan the database for unsent rows and try again. Implement this as a short loop that runs at a controlled cadence — for example, reading sensors every ten seconds and running the retry loop every minute. A common pitfall is continuously hammering a failing network endpoint; to avoid this, stop a retry batch on the first failure or implement exponential backoff. A concrete example is a function that queries rows with sent = 0 and attempts to POST them; on a successful HTTP 200, update sent to 1. Misconception: retries alone don't guarantee order; if ordering matters, include sequence numbers or rely on timestamps and idempotent server handling. Takeaway: the local database becomes a durable queue and the retry loop ensures eventual delivery when connectivity returns.

The process_unsent function demonstrates scanning unsent rows and attempting to send them to the cloud. The function selects rowid, timestamp, sensor_id, and value from sensor_readings where sent = 0. Understanding failure modes helps you choose retry behavior. Three common failure types are transient network blips, persistent endpoint errors, and local resource constraints. For transient blips, a simple periodic retry loop with short pauses is effective. For persistent errors like a server returning 5xx responses, the system should apply exponential backoff and alert operators if retries exceed thresholds. For local resource issues, such as low disk space, the Pi should stop collecting temporarily or rotate logs to avoid losing older data. A frequent misconception is to treat all failures the same — this leads to inefficient retries or lost observability. A small comparison: aggressive immediate retries on a downed endpoint waste power and bandwidth; controlled batching with backoff preserves resources and ships data when the server returns. Example: stop retrying on repeated failure and escalate to a log or LED indicator on the Pi, then resume normal retries after a longer wait. Takeaway: design retry strategies to match likely failure causes and preserve system health while ensuring eventual delivery. Separation of concerns states that collection, storage, and presentation should be distinct parts of your system. On the Raspberry Pi, keep the sensor read loop focused on capturing and persisting data, the storage layer focused on reliable writes and querying, and the presentation layer focused on rendering data for users or APIs. This separation reduces bugs: for example, if the dashboard slows down, it should not block sensor writes. A common error is coupling read loops with network uploads directly, which can cause missed readings when the network blocks. Instead, write to SQLite immediately and let a separate retry process handle uploads. This design also simplifies testing: you can test the read loop by verifying database inserts, test the retry loop by simulating failures and checking sent flags, and test the dashboard by mocking database queries. Practical example: run the sensor loop as a scheduled process or systemd service, run the retry loop on a cadence, and run Flask as a separate process. Takeaway: clear boundaries lead to safer failure modes and simpler debugging. These are the compact ideas to remember as you build a Raspberry Pi data logger. First, SQLite is a durable, serverless store suitable for edge logging; enable WAL mode for resilience. Second, buffering and retry turn the Pi into a reliable short‑term queue: write every reading, mark sent on success, and rescan unsent rows to ensure eventual delivery. Third, separation of concerns — keep collection, storage, and presentation distinct — prevents a slow dashboard from losing sensor reads and makes testing straightforward. Hold these concepts as rules of thumb when designing edge systems: prefer local durability, avoid coupling network operations to sampling, and keep your A P I outputs simple for charting clients. Misconception: do not assume uploads are instantaneous; design for delays and verify your system recovers without manual intervention.
